title: Digital Battle for Truth: Misinformation on Social Media and the Crisis of Youth Evangelisation in the Nigerian Catholic Church (Aduloju, International Journal of Developmental Issues in Education and Humanities 2(3), 2026)
screen_reason: Convergent mixed-methods study with a survey of 500 Nigerian Catholic youths. It reports shares of respondents who say they encounter religious misinformation on social media (75% high/very high exposure; platform-level shares) and a share who say they pass it on without verification (12.8%), which meet the RECALL (exposure and sharing) criteria.

estimates.platform: social media generally (WhatsApp, Facebook, TikTok, Instagram named elsewhere)
estimates.measure_type: % of Catholic youth respondents reporting high or very high exposure to religious misinformation on social media
estimates.value_raw: "a combined 75% of respondents report high or very high exposure" (Very High 35% + High 40%; Moderate 15%, Low 7%, Very Low 3%)
estimates.denominator: 500 Catholic youths surveyed via Google Forms across Nigeria's six geopolitical zones
estimates.definition: Respondent placed at the top two points ('high' or 'very high') of a five-point self-rated exposure scale for religious misinformation on social media
estimates.misinfo_def: no formal definition in the methods; the study measures encounters with "misleading religious content" / "unverified or misleading religious messages"
estimates.source_quote: The figure above shows that a combined 75% of respondents report high or very high exposure to religious misinformation, confirming that misinformation is a pervasive part of their daily social media encounters.
estimates.page_loc: Presentation of Results, Figure 1 (p. 216); repeated in Discussion (p. 219)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-rated five-point exposure scale; no definition of religious misinformation supplied to respondents, no external verification, no reliability statistics
estimates.moderator_quote: The quantitative part involved a survey of 500 young Catholics, distributed via Google Forms on online platforms, email, and parish youth centres.
estimates.notes: The 75% is stated verbatim in both the results and the discussion (not a sum computed by the extractor). Topic is religious misinformation, which has no codebook category: coded 'other'. Sampling is an online/parish convenience sample with no response rate. Year is the publication year; no fieldwork window is given.

estimates.measure_type: % of Catholic youth respondents naming WhatsApp as a platform on which religious misinformation reaches them
estimates.value_raw: "WhatsApp, with 82%, is the dominant channel for misinformation"
estimates.denominator: 500 Catholic youths surveyed via Google Forms across Nigeria's six geopolitical zones
estimates.definition: Respondent identified WhatsApp among the platforms responsible for spreading the religious misinformation they meet (multiple response; percentages sum to well over 100)
estimates.misinfo_def: no formal definition; "religious misinformation" / "unverified or misleading religious messages"
estimates.source_quote: Findings from the second research question indicate that WhatsApp (82%) is the most significant platform for the spread of religious misinformation among Catholic youth in Nigeria, followed by Facebook (70.8%), TikTok (59.2%), and Instagram (40.2%).
estimates.page_loc: Figure 2 (p. 217); Discussion, 'Platforms Responsible for Spreading Religious Misinformation' (p. 219)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-report, multiple-response platform item; item wording not published
estimates.moderator_quote: Figure 2: Research Question 2: Which platforms are most responsible for spreading religious misinformation among Catholic youth?
estimates.notes: Borderline and low confidence: the question is framed as which platforms are 'most responsible', so the item may be an attribution/perception question rather than a strict own-exposure question; the item wording is not published and the figure itself is mislabelled in the PDF (it reproduces the Figure 3 chart). Kept because the numbers are respondent shares split by platform.

estimates.measure_type: % of Catholic youth respondents who say they pass on religious messages without verifying them (the paper glosses this as sharing misinformation without checking)
estimates.value_raw: "12.8% still share misinformation without checking" / "12.8% share messages without verification"
estimates.denominator: 500 Catholic youths surveyed via Google Forms across Nigeria's six geopolitical zones
estimates.definition: Respondent chose 'share messages without verification' as their typical response to religious content encountered online (single-choice item: 35.2% ignore, 25.6% consult a priest, 20.4% cross-check with Catechism/Bible, 12.8% share unverified, 6% use fact-checking tools)
estimates.misinfo_def: no formal definition; "misleading religious content" / "unverified messages"
estimates.source_quote: The figure above shows that only 46% use reliable verification methods, while 35.2% ignore and scroll past, and 12.8% still share misinformation without checking.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-report of typical response behaviour; no behavioural data; item wording not published
estimates.moderator_quote: The data indicate that 35.2% of respondents ignore misleading content, 25.6% consult a priest or catechist, 20.4% cross-check with the Catechism or the Bible, 12.8% share messages without verification, and only 6% use online fact-checking tools.
estimates.notes: Borderline: the underlying item is 'share messages without verification', i.e. unverified sharing rather than verified sharing of false content; the paper itself glosses it as 'share misinformation without checking'. Coded RECALL/sharing on the paper's own gloss.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: the effects battery (42.8% confusion about Catholic teachings, 35.2% increased trust in online prophets, 31.6% syncretic beliefs, 26.4% doubts about Church authority, 14.8% strengthened faith, 19.2% no significant effect) - these are consequences of misinformation, not exposure/sharing shares. Also not extracted: verification behaviours (46% reliable verification, 25.6% consult clergy, 20.4% cross-check, 6% fact-checking tools), Church-response perceptions (40.8%, 32.4%, 23.6%, 11.2%, 29.6% see no visible response) and format preferences (47.6%, 42.4%, 39.2%, 32.8%, 16.8%). The PDF's figure images are not machine-readable and Figure 2 is mislabelled (it repeats the Figure 3 chart), so all values were taken from the verbatim text of the results and discussion. The qualitative strand (30 interviews, focus groups) yields no shares.

rob.design: Convergent mixed-methods: online survey of 500 self-selected Catholic youths recruited via Google Forms links, email and parish youth centres across six geopolitical zones (no sampling frame, no response rate, no demographic table), plus 30 purposive semi-structured interviews; descriptive percentages with unpublished item wording; no reliability or validity statistics; figures partly mislabelled.
rob.item6_quote: The findings reveal that exposure to religious misinformation is pervasive, with 75% of respondents reporting frequent encounters with misleading religious content, predominantly through WhatsApp, Facebook, and TikTok.
rob.item10_quote: The quantitative part involved a survey of 500 young Catholics ... The figure above shows that a combined 75% of respondents report high or very high exposure to religious misinformation.
